verses.text: Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, "This is the camp of God." So he named that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom.
He instructed them, "You are to say to my master Esau, 'Your servant Jacob says: I have been staying with Laban and have remained there until now.
I have oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants, and maidservants. I have sent this message to inform my master, so that I may find favor in your sight.'"
When the messengers returned to Jacob, they said, "We went to your brother Esau, and now he is coming to meet you—he and four hundred men with him."
In great fear and distress, Jacob divided his people into two camps, as well as the flocks and herds and camels.
He thought, "If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape."
Then Jacob declared, "O God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, the LORD who told me, 'Go back to your country and to your kindred, and I will make you prosper,'
I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. Indeed, with only my staff I came across the Jordan, but now I have become two camps.
Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid that he may come and attack me and the mothers and children with me.
But You have said, 'I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.'"
Jacob spent the night there, and from what he had brought with him, he selected a gift for his brother Esau:
200 female goats, 20 male goats, 200 ewes, 20 rams,
30 milk camels with their young, 40 cows, 10 bulls, 20 female donkeys, and 10 male donkeys.
He entrusted them to his servants in separate herds and told them, "Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds."
He instructed the one in the lead, "When my brother Esau meets you and asks, 'To whom do you belong, where are you going, and whose animals are these before you?'
then you are to say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau. And behold, Jacob is behind us.'"
He also instructed the second, the third, and all those following behind the herds: "When you meet Esau, you are to say the same thing to him.

You are also to say, 'Look, your servant Jacob is right behind us.'" For he thought, "I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me."
So Jacob's gifts went on before him, while he spent the night in the camp.
During the night Jacob got up and took his two wives, his two maidservants, and his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them across the stream, along with all his possessions.
So Jacob was left all alone, and there a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he struck the socket of Jacob's hip and dislocated it as they wrestled.
Then the man said, "Let me go, for it is daybreak." But Jacob replied, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
"What is your name?" the man asked. "Jacob," he replied.
Then the man said, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed."
And Jacob requested, "Please tell me your name." But he replied, "Why do you ask my name?" Then he blessed Jacob there.
So Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, "Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared."
The sun rose above him as he passed by Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip.
Therefore to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon which is at the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob's hip was struck near that tendon.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Isaac’s sons, Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:19 to 36:43)
context.audience: Israel, named for Jacob, learning how God kept His promise through a flawed and struggling family
context.setting: Angels of God meet Jacob, and he names the place Mahanaim, two camps (vv.1-2). He sends messengers to Esau in Seir, calling himself “your servant Jacob,” and hears that Esau is coming with four hundred men (vv.3-6). “In great fear and distress” he splits his household into two camps (vv.7-8) and prays his first long prayer: “I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. Indeed, with only my staff I came across the Jordan, but now I have become two camps. Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau” (vv.9-12). He sends ahead wave after wave of gifts, hundreds of goats, sheep, camels, cattle and donkeys, hoping to appease his brother (vv.13-21). At night he sends his family across the Jabbok, and “Jacob was left all alone, and there a man wrestled with him until daybreak” (vv.22-24). The man touches his hip and puts it out of joint, but Jacob holds on: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (vv.25-26). He is given a new name, “Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed” (v.28). Jacob names the place Peniel: “I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared” (v.30). He limps away into the sunrise (v.31).
context.custom: To ask someone’s name was to ask for a hold on them; Jacob gives his name, the heel-grabber, and receives a new one, but the stranger will not give his (v.29). The name Israel can be read as he struggles with God, or as God strives; the Hebrew verb sarah, to strive, is used again of Jacob in Hosea 12:3-4. The Jabbok (today’s Zarqa River) flows west through a deep gorge into the Jordan. The words for Jacob, Jabbok and wrestled (yaaqov, yabboq, yeaveq) sound alike in Hebrew.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 33 tells how Esau meets Jacob, not with a sword but with an embrace.
context.timelineBible: Hosea looks back: “In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God. Yes, he struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor” (Hosea 12:3-4). The new name becomes the name of the people, Israel. Jacob comes away blessed and limping: Paul learned that God’s “power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

translation.meaning: To wrestle, perhaps from the word for dust, avaq: to roll in the dust. Used only in this story.
To strive, to persist. The name Israel is built on it: you have struggled with God and with men, and prevailed.
Face, presence. Peniel means face of God. In the next chapter Jacob tells Esau that seeing his face is “like seeing the face of God” (33:10).

gospelParallels.note: My power is perfected in weakness.
Pray and do not lose heart.
No one has ever seen God; the one and only Son has made Him known.

otBackground.note: He struggled with the angel and prevailed.
No one can see My face and live.
Why do you ask My name?

mapCoords.placeName: Peniel and Mahanaim by the Jabbok (sites debated)

overview.summary: Afraid to meet Esau, Jacob prays, sends gifts ahead, and wrestles all night with a mysterious man at the Jabbok; he will not let go without a blessing and is renamed Israel.
overview.settingLine: Mahanaim and the ford of the Jabbok, east of the Jordan.
overview.placeName: Peniel and Mahanaim by the Jabbok (sites debated)

history.t: Esau comes with a small army.
A river later forming a border of Ammon and Gilead.

customs.t: A new name marked a new identity and calling.
Israel’s custom of not eating it is explained by this night (v.32).

archaeology.t: Twin mounds by the Jabbok are often proposed for Penuel and Mahanaim.
The modern Jabbok still cuts a deep valley through Gilead.

overview.discussion: Jacob refused to let go until he was blessed, and walked away limping (vv.26, 31). What would it look like for me to hold on to God in my struggle rather than run?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

peoplePlaces.d: Wrestles and blesses, but gives no name

historicalImage.caption: Jacob Wrestling with the Angel, by Rembrandt (about 1659, Gemäldegalerie, Berlin). The struggle looks almost like an embrace. “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26).
